newsitem.title: USA: Regulators grant wireless licenses with conditions.
newsitem.headline: Regulators grant wireless licenses with conditions.

text.p: Regulators Friday granted 63 licenses to the top bidder at last year's high-flying wireless phone auction, but on the condition that the company reduces its level of foreign ownership.

NextWave Personal Communications Inc. last May bid $4.2 billion at a Federal Communications Commission auction for 56 licenses to offer a new generation of cellular phone service throughout the country.
The auction of personal communications service (PCS) licenses raised a record $10.2 billion for the federal government.

NextWave -- a unit of privately held NextWave Telecom Inc. -- in July won seven additional PCS licenses worth $543 million. The FCC had reauctioned the permits after the winning bidders defaulted on payments.

Nextwave was the No. 1 bidder at both sales. But the winning bids in the first auction were challenged by two unsuccessful bidders, Antigone Communications LP and PCS Devco Inc. They argued that foreign ownership of Nextwave exceeded a 25 percent federal cap.
The FCC approval was conditioned on NextWave's restructuring its finances within six months so the company no longer exceeds the foreign ownership limit.

A variety of foreign conglomerates extended financing to NextWave, including Sony Corp. and Nippon Telegraph and Telephone of Japan and several big corporations from South Korea, such as Pohang Iron and Steel Co. Ltd.
"The arguments advanced in this proceeding raised difficult legal and financial issues," said Michele Farquhar, head of the FCC's wireless bureau.
"But having reviewed all the evidence, we believe that the decision to award these licenses on a conditional basis best serves the public interest and encourages new competition."
A spokeswoman for NextWave said the company's current ownership structure is about 3 percentage points over the 25 percent limit, based on an FCC review.
NextWave has submitted a plan to the agency to raise more domestic capital, possibly through a stock offering. It also could restructure its convertible debt.

PCS technology is expected to make the wireless phone a mass-market product, giving consumers several different communications services -- such as phone, paging, fax and Internet access -- through a hand-held device.
Nextwave said its licenses cover 40 of the top 50 markets in the nation, including New York, Los Angeles, Boston, Washington and Houston.
Meanwhile, the company hopes to complete two securities offerings in the first quarter, if market conditions permit.
The company has registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission to sell $150 million to $200 million worth of stock and $300 million to $400 million of high-yield bonds.
